title: Trump blames the messenger for the GOP’s problems | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump has locked on to a new excuse for the GOP’s impending 2026 midterm losses: It’s the messaging, not the results.

And the thing is, there is some truth in there — just not in the way Trump intends.

Trump has rolled out this purported explanation repeatedly over the last two days.

“We’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion and an extremely great job of running the country,” he said Wednesday at the White House.

“So I say we’ve done a bad public relations job, but a great management job – and that’s more important,” he added Thursday upon landing in Dallas.

Then at an event in Denton, Texas: “The only thing we’re doing badly at is public relations. In other words, we’re doing a phenomenal job, but … maybe we’re doing a bad job in selling it.”

The first thing to note is that this is well-trodden territory. Politicians often maintain their problem is not how great they are, but failing to make people understand that.

Kamala Harris said during the 2024 campaign that she and Joe Bidenhadn’t “taken adequate credit”for what they did. Barack Obama after the 2014 midterms called his team’s messaging problems a “failure of politics.” GOP vice-presidential candidate Paul Ryanargued much the sameafter his ticket’s loss in 2012.

And often, there is some truth in there.

But for Trump, this is more of a convenient excuse than anything else. He clearly has not only a messaging problem, but also a results problem — including on the issues voters indicate are most important to them.

And to the extent the messaging is the problem, it’s largely becausehismessaging — especially on the economy — is bad, counterproductive and hasn’t really changed.

There are credible arguments that the economy isn’t quite as bad as Americans think it is. But they fall flat for a simple reason, and it’s not that Trump and his party haven’t talked about it enough: Persistent inflation and high gas prices are constantly staring Americans in the face.

Trump got a boost in the 2024 election due to a spike in inflation during the Biden administration and amid the Covid-19 pandemic. But rather than drive down prices, like he promised to do instantly, he pursued unpopular policies that riskedexacerbatingthe problem — especially his global tariffs and the Iran war.

With those policies, Trumptook full ownership — more or less— of whatever happened next with the economy.

Inflation today (3.4%) is higher than it was when he took over (3%). And gas prices over $4 per gallon are a daily reminder of the direct costs to regular Americans of a war in Iran that Trump launched on his own but thatfew Americans see the point of.

The result: While just 44% of Americans blamed high prices mostly on Biden ahead of the 2022 midterm elections, according toAP-NORC polling, today 65% blame them mostly on Trump.

And a recentMarquette Law School pollshowed Americans said 64%-18% that Trump’s policy proposals would continue to increase inflation. Only 41% ofRepublicansthought they would decrease inflation.

And Trump has compounded these problems by how he talks about these issues.

First off, Trump made thegrave mistake of over-promising.

Hepromised gas under $2 per gallon; it’s over $4. He promised to bring down mortgage rates as low as under 3%; they’reover 7% and at their highest level since 2023. He promised to “cut your energy prices in half within 12 months”; energy priceshave continued to climb.

He also pledged to end the Russia-Ukraine war on Day One and said he was “not going to start a war” — both promises he’s broken.

Trump has always made lots of big promises, and people might overlook some of them. But not when it comes to their pocketbooks. Trump dropped the ball on the one thing he really needed to deliver on.

The second reason is his utter neglect and dismissal of inflation.

Rather than feeling Americans’ pain on price increases and putting forward plans to deal with the problem, he’s instead falsely claimed — ad nauseam — thatprices have actually been falling. (This despite Americans being able to see the truth in their everyday lives.) He’s bizarrely called affordability a “hoax.” He’s also made it abundantly clear he’s more interested inunpopular renovation projects in Washington— like ballrooms and reflecting pools and triumphal arches — than he is in addressing inflation.

Even as Trump has spoken dismissively of these issues, Vice President JD Vance hastried a different tack, arguing publicly and privately that Americans’ economic concerns should be taken seriously and dealt with. But Trump hasn’t echoed that.

And again, the polling bears out what a colossal problem this has become for his party.

CBS News pollinghas shown 78% of Americans said the Trump administration hasn’t focused enough on lowering prices. AndCNN pollinghas shown 73% said Trump “hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important problems.”

And the third reason is Trump’s and his team’s fixation on blaming Biden. But this argument went out the window long ago.

Trump has been in office now for 20 months and promised to deal with these problems quickly and easily. That’s already going to prompt less voter sympathy for the “I inherited this problem” argument. And then the president added to it with his economy-rocking policies.

I wrote about thisback in April 2025— shortly after Trump’s “Liberation Day” global tariffs announcement. Even then, anNPR-PBS-Marist College pollshowed 60% of Americans said the current economic conditions were mostly due to Trump’s policies, versus just 39% who said they were mostly “inherited.”

That was simply not the case with other recent presidents, including Trump in his first term. And that reinforced how he had anchored himself to whatever happened with the economy.

By the following month, aReuters-Ipsos pollshowed Americans said 59%-37% that if the country fell into a recession, it would be Trump’s fault rather than Biden’s.

If Americans reached these conclusions 17 or 18 months ago, are they really going to be suddenly convinced of the opposite? Of course not.

And that’s what makes the last few days telling.

Even as Trump has suddenly started complaining about the GOP’s messaging problems, he has doubled down on the same messages that got him into this mess. He spent much of an interview with Time magazineobsessing over the White House renovationsthat Americans hate. In Texas, he falsely claimed inflation was down and that his foes had suddenly invented the concept of affordability. And he and Vance have only ramped up their blame-Biden strategy.

None of it makes sense, and it hasn’t for some time. But rather than fix his political problem, Trump would rather blame the messenger — even ifheis both the poor messenger and the problem.
